text: This is a line chart showing validation loss during training across three different methods. The horizontal axis is training step, ranging from zero to ten thousand. The vertical axis is cross-entropy loss, ranging from one point five to four point five, and it does start at zero point zero. The legend lists three series: Baseline in blue, plus LoRA in orange, and Full fine-tune in green. All three curves start at the same validation loss of about four point five at training step zero. From there, all three lines decrease rapidly as training progresses. The baseline model in blue decreases the slowest, leveling off around step six thousand and remaining flat near two point one until the end at ten thousand steps. The plus LoRA model in orange decreases faster, reaching a value of about two point one at step four thousand and continuing to decrease gradually to about one point eight five at the end of training. The full fine-tune model in green drops the fastest and lowest, continuing a steady downward trend to reach about one point six three at ten thousand steps. Overall, full fine-tune achieves the lowest validation loss, followed by plus LoRA, with baseline performing the worst.

This is a bar chart titled ImageNet top-1 accuracy, which compares the performance of five different computer vision models. The vertical axis is labeled Top-1 accuracy in percent, ranging from 70 to 88, and it does not start at zero. The horizontal axis is labeled Model and lists five categories. There are five vertical bars representing the models. From left to right, their top-1 accuracy values are: ResNet-50 at 76.1 percent, ViT-B/16 at 81.8 percent, ConvNeXt-T at 82.1 percent, Swin-T at 81.3 percent, and Ours at 84.6 percent. Overall, the chart shows that the model labeled Ours achieves the highest top-1 accuracy at 84.6 percent, outperforming the other four models, while ResNet-50 performs the lowest at 76.1 percent. The remaining three models, ViT-B/16, ConvNeXt-T, and Swin-T, form a middle cluster with accuracies between 81.3 and 82.1 percent.

This grouped bar chart displays performance scores across three different benchmarks and three model sizes. The vertical axis represents the score, ranging from fifty to one hundred, and does not start at zero. The horizontal axis represents the benchmark, with three categories: GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD F1. The legend shows three model sizes: Small in blue, Base in orange, and Large in green. For the GLUE benchmark, the Small model scores about seventy-eight, the Base model scores about eighty-four, and the Large model scores about eighty-nine. For the SuperGLUE benchmark, the Small model scores sixty-five, the Base model scores about seventy-one, and the Large model scores about seventy-nine. For the SQuAD F1 benchmark, the Small model scores about eighty-three, the Base model scores about eighty-eight, and the Large model scores about ninety-one. Across all benchmarks, performance consistently increases as model size increases from Small to Base to Large. Additionally, SuperGLUE generally yields the lowest scores across all model sizes, while SQuAD F1 and GLUE achieve higher scores, with SQuAD F1 reaching the highest overall score of about ninety-one for the Large model.

This is a confusion matrix for a test set, showing the performance of a classification model across four classes. The horizontal axis is labeled Predicted label and lists cat, dog, bird, and car. The vertical axis is labeled True label and lists cat, dog, bird, and car from top to bottom. A vertical color bar on the right ranges from zero to over eighty, with darker shades of blue representing higher counts. For the true cat class, eighty-eight instances were correctly predicted as cat, nine as dog, two as bird, and one as car. For the true dog class, eleven were predicted as cat, eighty-four as dog, three as bird, and two as car. For the true bird class, three were predicted as cat, four as dog, ninety as bird, and three as car. For the true car class, zero were predicted as cat, one as dog, two as bird, and ninety-seven as car. The main pattern shows that the model performs best on the car class with ninety-seven correct predictions and very few misclassifications. The cat and dog classes show the highest confusion with each other, with eleven true dogs misclassified as cats and nine true cats misclassified as dogs. Overall, the diagonal elements contain the highest numbers for every class, indicating generally high accuracy across all four categories.

This is a heatmap displaying attention weights for Layer 6, Head 3 of a transformer model processing the sentence The cat sat on the mat. The vertical axis lists the query tokens, which are The, cat, sat, on, the, mat, and period, ordered from top to bottom. The horizontal axis lists the corresponding key tokens, in the same order from left to right. A vertical color bar on the right side represents attention values ranging from 0.0 to 1.0, where dark purple indicates low attention near 0.0 and bright yellow indicates high attention near 1.0. The attention matrix shows a clear autoregressive pattern, where each token primarily attends to itself and preceding tokens. Specifically, the diagonal elements show high attention weights, with The attending strongly to itself at 1.0, cat attending to itself at about 0.85, sat attending to itself at about 0.8, on attending to itself at about 0.8, the attending to itself at about 0.7, mat attending to itself at about 0.45, and the period attending to itself at about 0.65. Additionally, the query token mat displays a notable secondary attention weight of about 0.5 directed backward toward the key token cat. All other token pairs show very low attention weights close to 0.0, forming a dark triangular region above the diagonal.

This is a scatter plot showing model performance on the Mapped Multi-Task Language Understanding benchmark versus parameter count. The horizontal axis represents parameters in billions, ranging from roughly 5 to 70. The vertical axis represents Mapped Multi-Task Language Understanding percentage, ranging from 55 to 87, and the axis starts at 55 rather than zero. The legend categorizes data points into three families: dense models represented by blue circles, mixture of experts models represented by orange crosses, and distilled models represented by green squares. Overall, performance increases for all model families as parameter count increases, but mixture of experts models consistently achieve higher accuracy than dense or distilled models of similar parameter sizes. The lowest scores occur near six billion parameters, with dense and mixture of experts models both scoring around 56 percent. The highest scores reach approximately 87 percent Mapped Multi-Task Language Understanding around 65 billion parameters, achieved by both a dense and a mixture of experts model. Across almost all parameter sizes, mixture of experts models form the upper frontier of performance, while distilled models generally score lower than dense models at comparable parameter counts.

This box plot chart compares the inference latency across four different types of hardware. The vertical axis is labeled Latency in milliseconds, ranging from zero to one hundred seventy-five in increments of twenty-five, starting at zero. The horizontal axis is labeled Hardware and displays four categories: CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU. There are no sub-panels or legends. The categories from left to right show the distribution of latency measurements for each hardware type. The CPU has the highest latency, with a median of about one hundred sixteen milliseconds, a box spanning from about one hundred six to one hundred forty-one milliseconds, and whiskers extending from sixty-eight to one hundred ninety milliseconds. The GPU shows much lower latency, with a median of about sixteen milliseconds, a box from fourteen to twenty milliseconds, whiskers from ten to twenty-seven milliseconds, and one outlier at twenty-nine milliseconds. The TPU has the lowest latency, with a median of about twelve milliseconds, a box from ten to fourteen milliseconds, whiskers from seven to twenty milliseconds, and two outliers near twenty-four milliseconds. The Edge NPU has a median latency of about forty-four milliseconds, a box from thirty-eight to forty-eight milliseconds, whiskers from twenty-four to sixty-two milliseconds, and several outliers extending up to eighty-seven milliseconds. Overall, the TPU is the fastest hardware with the lowest latency, followed closely by the GPU, while the CPU is by far the slowest with the highest latency and the widest spread of results.

This is a grouped violin plot titled Effect of chain-of-thought prompting, comparing performance scores across three different tasks. The horizontal axis represents the task, with three categories labeled Math, Code, and Writing. The vertical axis represents the score, ranging from 20 to 100, starting from 20 rather than zero. The legend displays two conditions: Without CoT in blue on the left side of each violin, and With CoT in orange on the right side. Each violin contains three dashed horizontal lines representing the lower quartile, median, and upper quartile values. For the Math task, the Without CoT condition spans from about 25 to 80, with a median score of 55 and quartiles around 48 and 62. The With CoT condition for Math shifts noticeably higher, spanning from about 35 to over 105, with a median score of 74 and quartiles around 67 and 79. For the Code task, the Without CoT condition ranges from about 22 to 80 with a median of 55, while the With CoT condition ranges from about 25 to 98 with a median of 64. For the Writing task, both conditions overlap closely, with Without CoT showing a median of 54 and With CoT showing a median of 56, both spanning roughly from 22 to 86. Overall, chain-of-thought prompting provides the largest performance boost on Math, a moderate boost on Code, and almost no visible effect on Writing.

This is a histogram with overlaid kernel density estimation curves showing the distribution of logit margins. The horizontal axis is labeled Logit margin, ranging from about negative three to about five, starting at zero on the vertical axis. The vertical axis is labeled Count, ranging from zero to 175. The legend lists two categories: In-distribution in blue and Out-of-distribution in orange. The in-distribution data, shown in blue, is centered near zero with a peak count of about 175 and spans roughly from negative three to four. The out-of-distribution data, shown in orange, is shifted to the right, centered near three with a peak count of about 135 and spans roughly from one to five. The two distributions overlap between logit margin values of one and two.

This is a scatter plot with a linear regression trendline showing the relationship between compute and throughput. The horizontal axis is labeled GPU hours in thousands, ranging from zero to 10. The vertical axis is labeled Tokens/s in thousands, ranging from zero to 25. There are no other series, categories, or panels in this chart. The data points show a strong positive correlation, with a correlation coefficient of 0.94, and a blue trendline representing this relationship surrounded by a shaded confidence interval. The minimum observed values are near zero on the horizontal axis and around 2.5 on the vertical axis. The maximum observed values approach 10 thousand GPU hours on the horizontal axis and about 26 thousand tokens per second on the vertical axis. Overall, as GPU hours increase, throughput increases proportionally along a clear upward linear trend, with individual data points clustered tightly around the regression line.

This is a line chart showing the scaling of test error with data for three optimizers. The horizontal axis represents the dataset size in tokens, ranging from ten to the sixth power to ten to the tenth power on a logarithmic scale. The vertical axis represents the error, ranging from approximately zero point eight to three point two. The legend lists three optimizers: SGD in blue, Adam in orange, and Muon in green. For all three optimizers, the test error starts at about three point zero at a dataset size of ten to the sixth tokens. As the dataset size increases, the error for all optimizers decreases steadily. At the maximum dataset size of ten to the tenth tokens, the error for SGD finishes at about one point three four, Adam finishes at about one point one five, and Muon finishes at about zero point nine one. Overall, Muon consistently achieves the lowest error across all dataset sizes, followed by Adam in the middle, and SGD with the highest error.

This figure contains two line charts placed side by side, labeled (a) and (b), showing machine learning model performance. 

Chart (a) displays Accuracy on the vertical axis, ranging from about zero-point-two to one-point-zero, plotted against Epoch on the horizontal axis, which runs from zero to thirty. Chart (b) shows Final validation accuracy on the vertical axis, ranging from zero-point-six to zero-point-nine, plotted against Learning rate on the horizontal axis, which uses a logarithmic scale from ten to the negative fourth power to ten to the negative second power. 

Chart (a) includes a legend with two series: Train in blue and Validation in orange. A vertical dashed gray line marks epoch twelve. Chart (b) shows a single blue line with square markers at five data points corresponding to different learning rates.

In chart (a), both the train and validation accuracy start at about zero-point-two-six at epoch one and rise together. Around epoch twelve, where the dashed line is placed, the validation curve peaks at about zero-point-nine-two and then slowly decreases to about zero-point-eight-seven by epoch thirty. Meanwhile, the training accuracy continues to rise, approaching one-point-zero by epoch thirty. In chart (b), the final validation accuracy starts at zero-point-eight-one at a learning rate of ten to the negative fourth power, increases to a peak of zero-point-eight-nine at ten to the negative third power, and then drops sharply to zero-point-six-two at ten to the negative second power.

This figure consists of three line charts arranged side by side, showing accuracy curves per dataset over one hundred epochs. Each of the three panels plots accuracy on the vertical axis, ranging from zero to point eight, against epoch on the horizontal axis, ranging from zero to one hundred with grid lines every twenty-five epochs. The panels represent three different datasets: left is CIFAR-ten, middle is CIFAR-one hundred, and right is Tiny-ImageNet. The legend on the far right defines two augmentation methods: None is shown in blue, and RandAugment is shown in orange. Across all three datasets, both lines start at zero accuracy at epoch zero and increase rapidly before leveling off around epoch fifty to one hundred. For CIFAR-ten, the blue line representing no augmentation reaches a final accuracy of about zero point nine, while the orange line for RandAugment reaches about zero point nine four. For CIFAR-one hundred, the blue line ends around zero point six nine and the orange line ends near zero point seven five. For Tiny-ImageNet, the final accuracy is lower, with the blue line finishing at about zero point five five and the orange line at about zero point six. In every dataset, the orange line for RandAugment consistently achieves higher accuracy than the blue line after the first few epochs.

This is a dot plot with error bars showing an ablation study over five seeds, displaying BLEU performance across four model variants. The vertical axis represents BLEU, with values ranging from 57.5 to 72.5, and it does not start at zero. The horizontal axis represents the Variant, categorized into Full model, minus attention, minus residual, and minus norm. There is no legend. The key values for the mean BLEU score and standard deviation error bars are as follows. The Full model achieves the highest performance at about 71.5 BLEU, with error bars spanning from about 70.2 to 72.8. The minus attention variant drops to a mean of about 65.3 BLEU, with error bars from about 64.2 to 66.4. The minus residual variant performs the worst, plummeting to a mean of about 56.5 BLEU, with very narrow error bars from about 56.2 to 56.9. Finally, the minus norm variant recovers to a mean of about 66.6 BLEU, with error bars spanning from about 65.0 to 68.2. Overall, the full model achieves the best results, while removing the residual connections causes the most catastrophic performance drop, indicating that all components contribute to the model's performance, especially the residual connections.

This is a pair plot showing three features, petal length, petal width, and sepal length, grouped by three species categories. The figure is arranged as a three-by-three grid of panels. The diagonal panels show kernel density estimate distributions for each feature, while the off-diagonal panels are scatter plots displaying relationships between pairs of features. The horizontal and vertical axes correspond to the three features: petal length ranges from about one to seven, petal width ranges from zero to two point five, and sepal length ranges from four to eight. The legend on the right lists three species: setosa-like in blue, versicolor-like in orange, and virginica-like in green. In the diagonal panels, setosa-like has the lowest petal length and width values with peaks around one point five and zero point three, while virginica-like has the highest values with peaks around five point five and two. In the scatter plots, the data points clearly separate into three distinct clusters corresponding to the three species. The blue setosa-like points form a tight, isolated cluster on the lower end for petal length and width, whereas the orange versicolor-like and green virginica-like clusters are close to each other in sepal length but separate clearly along the petal length and petal width axes.

This image is a clustered heatmap titled Normalized task scores clustered, which visualizes the performance of five different models across six tasks. The vertical axis lists the models labeled M3, M4, M2, M1, and M5. The horizontal axis lists the tasks labeled Trans., Code, Math, Summ., QA, and NLI. A colorbar in the top left corner serves as a legend, ranging from dark blue at zero point five to dark red at one point zero, representing normalized task scores. 

Hierarchical clustering dendrograms are shown along the top and left sides, grouping similar tasks and models together. The tasks split into two main clusters: the first includes Translation, Code, and Math, while the second includes Summarization, QA, and NLI. The models also split into two main clusters: M3 and M4 in one group, and M2, M1, and M5 in another. 

Models M3 and M4 achieve their highest scores in the Code and Math tasks, shown in dark red and reddish tones with values near one point zero, while scoring poorly in QA and NLI, shown in dark blue. Conversely, models M1, M2, and M5 perform best on Summarization, QA, and NLI, with scores in the orange to red range, but show lower performance on Translation, Code, and Math, represented by blue shades. Model M3 achieves the absolute highest score for Code, shown in the darkest red, and the lowest score for NLI, shown in the darkest blue.

This is a cumulative distribution function plot showing response length distribution for two decoding methods. The horizontal axis is labeled Tokens generated, with a linear scale ranging from zero to sixteen hundred. The vertical axis is labeled Proportion, ranging from zero point zero to one point zero. The legend displays two decoding methods, Greedy in blue and Speculative in orange. Looking at the key values and patterns, the orange line for Speculative decoding rises much faster than the blue line for Greedy decoding, indicating that Speculative generates shorter responses overall. The orange line starts near zero tokens at zero proportion, reaches a proportion of about zero point five at around one hundred tokens, and nearly reaches one point zero at about four hundred tokens, with its absolute maximum ending around eight hundred tokens. In contrast, the blue line for Greedy decoding starts near zero tokens, reaches a proportion of zero point five around two hundred fifty tokens, and reaches one point zero around sixteen hundred tokens, showing a much wider spread and longer maximum response lengths compared to the speculative method.

This is a horizontal bar chart showing the count of papers in a survey categorized by six different publication venues. The vertical axis lists the venues from top to bottom as NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, CVPR, and EMNLP. The horizontal axis represents the count, starting at zero and ranging up to 450 with grid lines every 50 units. Reading the count values for each venue: NeurIPS has about 410 papers, ICML has about 305 papers, ICLR has about 375 papers, ACL has about 158 papers, CVPR has about 290 papers, and EMNLP has about 132 papers. NeurIPS has the highest number of papers in the survey, closely followed by ICLR. ICML and CVPR form a middle tier with around 300 papers each. ACL and EMNLP have the lowest counts, both falling below 160 papers.
